lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- When the Faces Go Blank
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Joyce Michalczuk | Lesson 4 -- When the Faces Go Blank

listenings.text: I have presented to teams in Germany, in India and in Japan, and for years I made the same mistake. I saw a quiet room, no smiles, nobody nodding, and I panicked. I started to explain everything again, faster, and that was the moment I really lost them. Later I learned that a blank face is not always a confused face. In many cultures people listen in silence. It means respect, not trouble. So now, when the faces go blank, I do not speed up. I slow down, I finish my sentence, and I wait two seconds. Very often somebody asks a good question, and that question tells me exactly where they are.

I run a finance team across four countries, and I do not trust a quiet room. Silence on a video call can mean anything. People are reading email, the connection is bad, or they are lost and too polite to say it. So I check, every few minutes. But I never ask, does that make sense? Everybody says yes to that question. I ask something specific. Which part should I go over again? Or, what would this mean for your team? If nobody can answer, I did not explain it well, and I say it again in a different way. Not louder. Different.
